about: Batch 4: 19 events and spans from 1800 to 1975 plus Ashoka's reign, covering Napoleonic Europe, Qing China, Meiji Japan, the US Civil War, World Wars I and II, the Cold War, Korean and Vietnam Wars, US Civil Rights, the Space Race, and the Indian Independence Movement. Pre-sorted by Claude: seven text fixes, Cold War importance 8, id 'indian-nationalist-movement'; links reworked to slot the new battles into the existing WWI and WWII sequences.

events.name: Napoleon Crowned Emperor
aliases: Napoleon I becomes Emperor of the French
events.description: First Consul Napoleon Bonaparte is crowned Emperor of the French at Notre-Dame Cathedral in Paris in the presence of Pope Pius VII, replacing the French Consulate with the First French Empire.
events.note: 2 December 1804. Note: Napoleon placed the crown on his own head after Pius VII anointed him, though accounts of whether he took the crown from the pope's hands vary slightly.
events.significance: The coronation transformed revolutionary France into a hereditary empire and signaled that Napoleon intended to rule as an equal to Europe's established monarchs. Combined with his territorial reorganizations in Italy and Germany, it helped provoke Britain, Austria and Russia to form the Third Coalition.

events.name: Treaty of Nanking
aliases: Cession of Hong Kong to Britain
events.description: Qing and British representatives sign a peace treaty aboard HMS Cornwallis at Nanjing, ending the First Opium War, opening five Chinese treaty ports to foreign trade, imposing a silver indemnity and ceding Hong Kong Island to Britain.
events.note: 29 August 1842. [Claude at review: Extraterritoriality came in the 1843 supplementary treaty (Bogue), not Nanking itself.]
events.significance: Known in China as the first of the unequal treaties, the agreement dismantled the Canton trade system and, with a supplementary treaty the next year, eroded Qing tariff and judicial sovereignty, and established Hong Kong as a British crown colony until its handover to China in 1997.

events.name: Commodore Perry Arrives in Japan
aliases: Black Ships arrive in Edo Bay
events.description: United States Navy Commodore Matthew Perry steams into Edo Bay with four armed warships, delivering a letter from President Millard Fillmore demanding that the Tokugawa shogunate open Japanese ports to American trade and diplomacy.
events.note: 8 July 1853 (first arrival at Uraga; Perry returned in February 1854 to sign the Convention of Kanagawa). Note that Japan maintained limited trade with the Dutch and Chinese at Nagasaki during sakoku, so avoid saying Japan was completely sealed off.
events.significance: Perry's gunboat diplomacy forced the Tokugawa shogunate to sign the Convention of Kanagawa and unequal commercial treaties with Western powers. The resulting political crisis discredited the shogunate among samurai reformers and helped set off the Meiji Restoration.

events.name: Battle of Fort Sumter
aliases: First shots of the American Civil War
events.description: Confederate artillery under General P. G. T. Beauregard bombards the federal garrison at Fort Sumter in Charleston Harbor, South Carolina, forcing Major Robert Anderson to surrender the fort after thirty-four hours of shelling.
events.note: 12–13 April 1861. No soldiers were killed during the bombardment itself, though two Union soldiers died during the surrender salute.
events.significance: The bombardment turned the secession crisis into open warfare, opening the American Civil War. President Abraham Lincoln immediately called for seventy-five thousand state militia volunteers to suppress the rebellion, prompting Virginia, Arkansas, Tennessee and North Carolina to secede and join the Confederacy.

events.name: Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand
events.description: Bosnian Serb nationalist Gavrilo Princip shoots and kills Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, and his wife Sophie during an official visit to Sarajevo in Bosnia and Herzegovina.
events.significance: The killings set off the July Crisis, during which Austria-Hungary issued an ultimatum to Serbia and declared war a month later. Europe's interlocking alliance systems rapidly drew Germany, Russia, France and Britain into the First World War.

events.name: Gandhi Returns to India
aliases: Mahatma Gandhi returns from South Africa
events.description: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi returns permanently to Bombay after more than two decades practicing law and leading civil rights campaigns in South Africa, touring British India on the advice of Gopal Krishna Gokhale to study conditions firsthand.
events.note: 9 January 1915 (commemorated in India as Pravasi Bharatiya Divas).
events.significance: Gandhi brought his method of nonviolent mass resistance, satyagraha, from South Africa into Indian nationalist politics. Through early local campaigns in Champaran and Kheda, he forged direct ties with peasants and workers and soon emerged as the central leader of the independence movement.

events.name: Battle of the Somme
events.description: British and French armies launch a massive joint offensive against fortified German trenches along the Somme River in northern France, suffering staggering casualties on the opening day and grinding forward for four months.
events.note: 1 July to 18 November 1916. Total casualties exceeded one million across all sides, including about 57,470 British casualties on 1 July alone. Tanks were used in combat for the first time during the battle in September 1916.
events.significance: Although Allied forces gained only about six miles of territory, the offensive relieved German pressure on the French army at Verdun and severely depleted experienced German infantry units. The Somme also saw the first battlefield deployment of tanks and became a lasting symbol of industrial trench warfare's human cost.

events.name: United States Enters World War I
aliases: American entry into World War I
events.description: Following Germany's resumption of unrestricted submarine warfare and the interception of the Zimmermann Telegram proposing a German-Mexican alliance, the United States Congress declares war on Germany at President Woodrow Wilson's request.
events.note: 6 April 1917 (declared war on Austria-Hungary on 7 December 1917). [Claude at review: US troops played a modest part in stopping the spring offensives; their weight told later in 1918.]
events.significance: American entry supplied the exhausted Allied powers with vital credit, munitions, naval escorts and eventually two million fresh troops in France, helping turn the tide against Germany in 1918. It also positioned President Woodrow Wilson to shape the postwar Versailles settlement and the League of Nations.

events.name: Battle of Stalingrad
events.description: German and Axis forces assault the industrial city of Stalingrad on the Volga River, becoming locked in brutal close-quarters urban combat before the Soviet Red Army launches Operation Uranus to encircle and destroy the German Sixth Army.
events.note: 23 August 1942 to 2 February 1943 (filed under 1942 as specified in the gap list). Total military and civilian casualties are estimated at around two million. [Claude at review: Germany counterattacked in early 1943 (Kharkov); the initiative passed for good after Kursk, July 1943.]
events.significance: Stalingrad is widely seen as the turning point of the war in Europe: it destroyed an entire German field army and ended Germany's drive toward the Caucasus oilfields. After the Soviet victory at Kursk that summer, the Red Army held the initiative all the way to Berlin.

events.name: Battle of Midway
aliases: US Navy defeats Japan at Midway
events.description: United States Navy carrier forces, forewarned by naval codebreakers of an impending Japanese ambush, sink four Imperial Japanese fleet carriers and a heavy cruiser near Midway Atoll in the central Pacific.
events.note: 4–7 June 1942. The US lost the carrier USS Yorktown, while Japan lost Akagi, Kaga, Soryu and Hiryu.
events.significance: Midway crippled Japan's offensive naval air power, permanently shifting the strategic balance in the Pacific War. Unable to replace its lost fleet carriers and veteran aircrews at the pace of American industrial production, Japan was forced onto the defensive for the remainder of the war.

events.name: Germany Surrenders (V-E Day)
events.description: Following Adolf Hitler's suicide and the Soviet capture of Berlin, German military leaders sign instruments of unconditional surrender at Reims and Berlin, ending World War II in Europe.
events.note: Act of surrender signed at Reims on 7 May 1945 and ratified in Berlin late on 8 May (early 9 May Moscow time, hence Victory Day on 9 May in Russia).
events.significance: Germany's surrender ended nearly six years of war in Europe, liberated Nazi-occupied nations and halted the Holocaust. Allied armies divided Germany and Austria into occupation zones, setting the geopolitical boundary across central Europe that soon hardened into the Cold War.

events.name: Korean Armistice Agreement
events.description: Representatives of the United Nations Command, North Korea and China sign an armistice at Panmunjom, halting three years of fighting in the Korean War and establishing the Korean Demilitarized Zone near the thirty-eighth parallel.
events.note: 27 July 1953. South Korea's Syngman Rhee refused to sign the agreement, and no formal peace treaty was ever concluded, leaving the two Koreas technically at war.
events.significance: The armistice ended active combat in a war that had killed roughly three million people, while leaving the Korean Peninsula divided along a heavily fortified border. Because no formal peace treaty followed, the Demilitarized Zone remained a permanent Cold War flashpoint.

events.name: Voting Rights Act Signed
aliases: Voting Rights Act signed into law
Lyndon Johnson signs Voting Rights Act
events.description: President Lyndon B. Johnson signs landmark federal civil rights legislation outlawing literacy tests and other discriminatory barriers that disenfranchised African American voters, while authorizing federal oversight of voter registration in jurisdictions with histories of discrimination.
events.significance: Within months, federal examiners registered hundreds of thousands of Black voters across the American South, dismantling Jim Crow disenfranchisement in practice. The surge in Black voter registration transformed Southern politics and led to the election of thousands of African American local, state and federal officials.

events.name: Apollo-Soyuz Test Project
events.description: An American Apollo spacecraft and a Soviet Soyuz capsule dock in Earth orbit, allowing astronauts Thomas Stafford, Vance Brand and Deke Slayton to shake hands and conduct joint experiments with cosmonauts Alexei Leonov and Valeri Kubasov.
events.note: Docking occurred on 17 July 1975 (mission ran 15–24 July 1975). Many historians treat it as the symbolic end of the Cold War Space Race. [Claude at review: A common reading, not a fact: our Space Race span ends with the Moon landing in 1969.]
events.significance: As the first international crewed spaceflight, the mission symbolized Cold War detente and is often taken as the symbolic end of the US-Soviet Space Race. Its compatible docking system and joint operational procedures laid technical foundations for later cooperation aboard Mir and the International Space Station.

events.name: Fall of Saigon
events.description: North Vietnamese and Viet Cong forces capture Saigon, the capital of South Vietnam, as American helicopters complete the emergency evacuation of remaining US personnel and thousands of South Vietnamese allies from the city.
events.note: 30 April 1975. The city was renamed Ho Chi Minh City.
events.significance: Saigon's capture ended the Vietnam War and led to the formal reunification of Vietnam under communist rule in 1976. The conflict left millions of Vietnamese dead, triggered a massive refugee exodus across Southeast Asia and reshaped American foreign policy and public trust for decades.

spans.name: Reign of Ashoka
spans.description: The rule of the third Mauryan emperor over almost all of the Indian subcontinent except the far south, marked by the Kalinga War, Ashoka's embrace of Buddhism and his empire-wide rock and pillar edicts promoting dhamma.
spans.note: Conventional dates c. 268 to 232 BCE (coronation around 268 BCE after a succession struggle following Bindusara's death in c. 272 BCE). [Claude at review: The Tamil south stayed independent.] [Claude at review: His Rock Edict XIII names the Hellenistic kings; Central Asian missions are not attested.]
spans.significance: Ashoka's rock and pillar edicts provide the earliest decipherable royal inscriptions in South Asia and articulated an ethic of nonviolence, religious tolerance and public welfare. By sending Buddhist envoys to Sri Lanka and, by his own account, to the Hellenistic kingdoms of the west, he helped transform Buddhism into a major world religion.

spans.name: War of the Third Coalition
spans.description: The opening conflict of the Napoleonic Wars, pitting Napoleon's French Empire against Britain, Austria, Russia, Naples and Sweden across naval battles at Trafalgar and land campaigns at Ulm and Austerlitz.
spans.note: 1803 (Britain declares war on France in May 1803; Austria and Russia join the coalition in 1805) to 1806 (Treaty of Pressburg signed December 1805; fighting in Naples and Dalmatia continues into 1806).
spans.significance: While Britain's naval victory at Trafalgar secured British mastery of the seas, Napoleon's decisive triumphs at Ulm and Austerlitz shattered the Third Coalition on land. The resulting Peace of Pressburg led directly to the dissolution of the thousand-year-old Holy Roman Empire in 1806.

spans.name: Indian Independence Movement
spans.description: The decades-long political, mass-mobilization and revolutionary struggle against British colonial rule in India, spanning early constitutional agitation, the Swadeshi campaign, Gandhian civil disobedience and final negotiations for independence.
spans.note: Dated from the founding of the Indian National Congress in 1885 (some historians begin with the 1857 Rebellion) to independence and Partition in August 1947. Uses id 'indian-nationalist-movement' because 'indian-independence-movement' already exists for the 1920–1947 Gandhian era. [Claude at review: id changed from '-full' to describe the subject.]
spans.significance: Culminating in the end of the British Raj and the creation of India and Pakistan, the movement pioneered mass nonviolent civil disobedience as a political force. Its success inspired anticolonial movements across Asia and Africa and accelerated the postwar dismantling of European empires.

spans.name: Cold War
spans.description: The decades-long geopolitical, ideological and nuclear rivalry between the United States and its allies and the Soviet Union and its allies, waged through proxy wars, alliance blocs, espionage and arms and space races without direct superpower combat.
spans.note: 1947 (Truman Doctrine and Marshall Plan) to 1991 (dissolution of the Soviet Union). [Claude at review: importance 8, level with World War II.] [Claude at review: Afghanistan and Central America were not decolonization conflicts.]
spans.significance: The Cold War divided Europe with the Iron Curtain, drove nuclear deterrence and space exploration, and turned conflicts from Korea and Vietnam to Afghanistan and Central America into proxy wars. Its end left the United States as the sole superpower and reshaped international institutions worldwide.
